summary: Psalm 134 is a very short Song of Ascents. It first calls Yahweh’s servants, who stand by night in Yahweh’s house, to praise him with lifted hands in the sanctuary. It then answers with a blessing from Zion, naming Yahweh as the maker of heaven and earth.
whyItMatters: This psalm closes the Songs of Ascents with praise and blessing at the sanctuary. It gathers pilgrimage, temple service, and creation into three compact verses without explaining the exact occasion.

context.author: Unknown. Psalms is an anthology with many writers and collections, and this psalm’s heading identifies it as a Song of Ascents rather than naming an author.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping community, especially readers or singers who know the language of temple service and pilgrimage; later Jewish and Christian communities also received it as prayer and song.
context.date: Uncertain. Individual psalms may come from different periods from the monarchy through the postexilic period, and assigning one date to the whole Psalter would be misleading.
context.setting: Book V of Psalms, within the Songs of Ascents. The poem is oriented toward Yahweh’s house, the sanctuary, and Zion.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry and prayer, using summons and blessing in a three-verse liturgical shape.

outline.heading: Call to the night servants
outline.note: The psalm opens as a Song of Ascents and addresses Yahweh’s servants who stand by night in Yahweh’s house.

outline.heading: Gesture of praise
outline.note: The servants are told to lift up their hands in the sanctuary and praise Yahweh.

outline.heading: Blessing from Zion
outline.note: The final line asks Yahweh, the maker of heaven and earth, to bless from Zion.

keyVerses.text: A Song of Ascents. Look! Praise Yahweh, all you servants of Yahweh, who stand by night in Yahweh’s house!
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the psalm its setting and address: a Song of Ascents speaking to Yahweh’s servants in Yahweh’s house at night.

keyVerses.text: Lift up your hands in the sanctuary. Praise Yahweh!
keyVerses.why: This is the central action requested in the psalm: bodily, voiced praise in the sanctuary.

keyVerses.text: May Yahweh bless you from Zion, even he who made heaven and earth.
keyVerses.why: The psalm ends by moving from human praise to Yahweh’s blessing, and it identifies Yahweh as creator of heaven and earth.

themes: Yahweh as maker of heaven and earth

questions.question: What is a Song of Ascents?
questions.answer: The heading places this psalm among the Songs of Ascents, the group running from Psalm 120 through Psalm 134. The collection includes songs of going to Yahweh’s house, and this final poem addresses servants worshiping there. It does not specify the exact journey or ceremony behind the title.

questions.question: Who are the servants of Yahweh in this psalm?
questions.answer: The verse addresses people who “stand by night in Yahweh’s house.” The chapter does not name them more specifically. Readers often connect the wording with temple service, but the psalm itself keeps the address brief.

questions.question: Why does the psalm mention night?
questions.answer: Verse 1 says the servants stand by night in Yahweh’s house. The detail gives the praise a setting after dark, but the chapter does not describe a full schedule or ritual. It is enough for the poem that praise belongs even in the night watch.

questions.question: What does lifting hands mean here?
questions.answer: Verse 2 commands the servants to lift up their hands in the sanctuary and praise Yahweh. The gesture is presented as part of worship, but the psalm does not explain one fixed posture or rule for every setting. It shows embodied praise in the sanctuary.

questions.question: What is the sanctuary?
questions.answer: In this chapter, the sanctuary is the place where the servants lift their hands and praise Yahweh. Verse 1 has already mentioned Yahweh’s house, so the wording points readers toward the temple-oriented setting of the poem. The psalm does not pause to describe the building.

questions.question: Why does the blessing come from Zion?
questions.answer: Verse 3 asks Yahweh to bless “from Zion.” In Psalms, many poems are oriented toward Jerusalem and its temple, and this psalm’s own references to Yahweh’s house, the sanctuary, and Zion fit that setting. The line presents Zion as the place from which blessing is invoked, not as an explanation of all later ideas about Zion.

questions.question: Why does the psalm call Yahweh the one who made heaven and earth?
questions.answer: The final phrase identifies the one who blesses as creator. That makes the blessing larger than a local wish, even though it is spoken from Zion. The chapter holds temple language and creation language together in one closing line.

questions.question: Is this psalm spoken by pilgrims to temple servants, or by servants to the people?
questions.answer: Verses 1–2 address Yahweh’s servants in the sanctuary, while verse 3 pronounces a blessing on “you.” This change can be heard as an exchange, with visitors calling the servants to praise and a blessing spoken in reply. The poem names neither the visitors nor a new speaker, however, so that performance arrangement remains a possibility rather than a stated fact.

questions.question: Why is the psalm so short?
questions.answer: Psalm 134 is complete in three verses: summons, gesture, and blessing. Psalms often use compressed poetry, where a few lines can carry setting, action, and theology without connective explanation. This chapter’s brevity is part of its force.

glossary.def: The heading shared by Psalms 120-134. In this chapter it marks the psalm as part of that collection, without explaining the title’s exact performance setting.
The people addressed in verse 1, described as those who stand by night in Yahweh’s house.
The worship place named in verse 2, where the addressed servants are told to lift up their hands and praise Yahweh.
The place named in verse 3 as the source from which Yahweh’s blessing is requested.
The created totality named in verse 3, identifying Yahweh as maker of all rather than only the God of one shrine.
